summary: Describes extensions to OSPF version 2 for intra-area traffic engineering, carried in Opaque Link State Advertisements. They let routers advertise extra link information that supports choosing paths based on more than simple shortest distance. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3630 extends OSPF Version 2 so routers can share extra information about links, including bandwidth and administrative groups. The information is flooded within an OSPF area and can support traffic-engineering path choices. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4203 and RFC 5786.

subtitle: How OSPF routers share link attributes for traffic engineering within an area.

tldr.problem: OSPF's ordinary link information does not include all attributes needed to select paths using traffic-engineering constraints such as bandwidth or administrative groups.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3630 carries traffic-engineering data in area-scoped type 10 Opaque LSAs, using Router Address and Link TLVs with link-attribute sub-TLVs.
tldr.outcome: Routers can build a traffic-engineering database without changing normal OSPF route calculations. RFC 3630 updates RFC 2370 and has itself been updated by RFC 4203 and RFC 5786.

today: RFC 3630 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 2370 and has itself been updated by RFC 4203 and RFC 5786.

sections.title: Extra Link Information for Traffic Engineering
sections.content:
RFC 3630 adds traffic-engineering (TE) information to OSPF Version 2. The extensions describe link attributes, such as bandwidth and administrative groups, and distribute them within an OSPF area. A router can build a TE database from this information and use it to monitor links or calculate paths subject to constraints.

The RFC covers intra-area distribution only. It does not define traffic engineering across areas or autonomous systems, and it does not support unnumbered links. Reservation state for multi-access links may be inaccurate when more than two devices share the network. Routers without TE support must still flood these type 10 Opaque LSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers can share extra facts about links, such as available bandwidth, within an area. A router can use those facts to choose paths that meet additional requirements.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering LSAs and TLVs
sections.content:
The extensions use type 10 Opaque Link State Advertisements (LSAs), which have area flooding scope. The TE LSA uses opaque type 1. Its remaining 24-bit Instance field allows a system to originate multiple TE LSAs; the LSA ID does not describe topology.

The LSA payload contains one top-level Type-Length-Value (TLV). RFC 3630 defines a Router Address TLV and a Link TLV. TLVs carry nested values, are padded to four-octet alignment, and do not count padding in their length. Nested TLVs are also aligned, and routers ignore types they do not recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: A router sends TE information in an area-scoped Opaque LSA. The LSA contains a labeled Router Address or Link value, and receivers can skip labels they do not recognize.

sections.title: Router Addresses and Link Attributes
sections.content:
The Router Address TLV carries a stable IP address for the advertising router. It must appear in exactly one TE LSA from that router. The address can help identify the same router when both OSPF and IS-IS TE information are combined.

Each Link TLV describes one link and contains sub-TLVs in any order. Link Type and Link ID are required exactly once. Other defined attributes include local and remote interface addresses, a TE metric, maximum bandwidth, maximum reservable bandwidth, unreserved bandwidth at priorities 0 through 7, and an administrative-group bit mask. Bandwidth values are in bytes per second.
sections.plainLanguage: A Router Address identifies a router, while a Link TLV describes one link. The link data can report its type, neighbor, metric, bandwidth and administrative groups.

sections.title: Flooding Updates and Building the TE Database
sections.content:
Routers originate TE LSAs when their contents change and when OSPF otherwise requires an update, such as a refresh. Implementations may use thresholds to decide which changes trigger immediate flooding, and should rate-limit origination to at most one TE LSA every MinLSInterval.

When a router receives a changed TE LSA or Network LSA, it updates its traffic-engineering database. No Shortest Path First or other route calculation is needed for that update.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers send updated TE information when link data changes, subject to rate limits. Receivers update their TE database without recalculating ordinary routes.

sections.title: Routers Without Traffic-Engineering Support
sections.content:
The RFC expects routers that do not implement the extensions to ignore Opaque LSAs without causing interoperability problems. Because those routers do not use the additional information, the traffic-engineering topology may have missing pieces.

If the resulting topology remains connected, TE paths can still be calculated and are expected to work. This does not make the missing link attributes available to the calculation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that do not use TE information can ignore these LSAs. A TE database may then be incomplete, though a connected topology can still support path calculations.

sections.title: Protecting Traffic-Engineering Information
sections.content:
Opaque LSAs are not used for Shortest Path First calculation or normal IP routing, so these extensions do not change IP routing itself. However, altering TE LSAs can affect traffic-engineering calculations.

The RFC recommends applying the mechanisms used to secure ordinary OSPF LSA transmission to all Opaque LSAs, including TE LSAs. It notes that the referenced OSPF security mechanisms apply to Opaque LSAs and suggests that future OSPFv2 authentication mechanisms cover them too.
sections.plainLanguage: False TE information can lead a traffic-engineering calculation to choose a different path, even though it does not change normal IP routing. The RFC recommends protecting TE LSAs like other OSPF LSAs.

sections.title: Allocating LSA and Sub-TLV Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers top-level TE LSA types and sub-TLV types. For top-level types, values from 3 through 32767 require Standards Action. Values from 32768 through 32777 are for experimental use and are not registered; values from 32778 through 65535 are held until a Standards Track RFC specifies their assignment.

Sub-TLV assignment follows the same rules, except Standards Action applies from 10 through 32767. The experimental and reserved ranges have the same boundaries as for top-level types.
sections.plainLanguage: Different number ranges have different rules for assigning new TE labels. Some require Standards Action, some are for experiments, and some remain unassigned until a standards document covers them.
